name_ru: Цянь Вэй Мо Ли Хуа Ча
cultivar: Mingshan 131, Mingshan 311, Fuxuan 9, local Sichuan population
processing: A green tea base is refined, then scented with fresh jasmine. Its signature steps are selecting the blossoms by hand and pan-firing flowers with the tea at 80 to 100°C, which is what gives the regional 'cooked' fragrance.
harvest_season: Base tea is picked from early March to the end of May, as single buds up to one bud with two opening leaves.
appearance_dry: Fine, tight curls or slim strips, downy and fresh dark green, with visible dried white blossoms.
appearance_liquor: Pale, tender green and very clear.
taste_profile: Strong, fresh-sweet jasmine over a smooth, sweet green tea, with a warm cooked note that sets it apart from cleaner jasmine styles.

brewing.notes: Too hot or too long pulls bitterness from the base before the perfume has had time to show. Use a lidded cup and smell it between steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest and grade, and the freshest is worth seeking out: as with most jasmine teas, the scent fades with storage, so drink it within a year or so. The appellation also describes different flavour styles, including clear, strong and mixed-aroma, so ask which one a lot belongs to.
description:
Qianwei jasmine is the scented green tea of Qianwei County in Leshan. Its point of difference is a fuller, warm scent known locally as 'cooked fragrance'.

That comes from an unusual step. Beyond standard scenting with the local Jinjian (金犍) jasmine and other sharp- or multi-petalled kinds, makers pick apart the opening blooms and pan-fire them with the tea at 80 to 100°C. Many blossoms remain in the finished tea, so do not be surprised by white petals in the bag.

The cup is pale and clean, with a sweet base and plenty of jasmine. Local descriptions say the character moves with the season, from clear in spring tea to pear-like in summer, mellow in autumn and lotus-like in winter. Keep steeps short at first, as the scent comes out early.

Buy the most recent lot you can find and smell it first. A bright, natural floral note is the goal; a sharp, perfumed edge suggests flavouring rather than real flowers. The protected name applies only to tea made within Qianwei County.
history:
Little is documented about when jasmine scenting began in Qianwei. Local accounts call it a traditional tea created by local growers, without giving firm dates.

The recorded milestone is recent: national geographical indication protection was approved on 15 December 2010, with a technical standard that sets its cultivars, picking window and flower-firing step.
